title: CDI Listening Test 41
description: A full Listening test from the CDI practice materials, with the original recording. 4 parts, 40 questions.
topics: Robert phones Medical Help Direct in the middle of the night about back pain
A school principal talks to parents about an upcoming three-day trip to an outdoor education centre
Liz from New Zealand and Scott from the UK plan a presentation about Stone Point, a historical site in New Zealand
A lecture on the Berber peoples of North Africa and the nomadic Tuaregs of the Sahara

parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: Robert phones Medical Help Direct in the middle of the night about back pain.

groups.answerRule: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A school principal talks to parents about an upcoming three-day trip to an outdoor education centre.

questions.text: A trip to the outdoor education centre will help the children
questions.explanation: "We strongly believe children should be encouraged to try different things and not give up when it gets difficult." — react positively to new challenges (C).

questions.text: To prepare their children for the trip, parents should

options.text: let them try sleeping in a tent at home
make sure they get enough sleep before they leave
tell them that they will be in a tent with their friends

questions.explanation: "You can do this just by making sure they have some early nights before we go." — make sure they get enough sleep (B).

questions.text: What do parents need to put in their children's backpack?
questions.explanation: "What we do need in the backpacks are bags for cleaning up and for wet clothing, so plastic ones." — plastic bags (A). Biscuits go in the box; no money.

questions.text: What are children allowed to bring on the trip?
questions.explanation: "Cell phones are permitted, but they must be switched off at night." Penknives provided by centre; electronic games banned.

questions.text: How are parents selected to attend the trip?

options.text: The first ten parents to sign up will be able to go.
Parents' names will be chosen from a box.
Preference will be given to parents with camping skills.

questions.explanation: "If you are absolutely sure you can come, put your name down on the sign up form and the first ten will be asked to come."

questions.text: Payment for the trip

options.text: must be handed to the child's teacher.
can be left at the school office.
should be made directly to the outdoor education centre.

questions.explanation: "Payment to the centre is made by school, not by parents." — the school pays the centre directly (C). Parents can leave payment at office or use bank details.

questions.text: Woodcarving studio

▶ 07:14Principal: At the school, we strongly believe children should be encouraged to try different things and not give up when it gets difficult. And that's what the center is all about, having a go.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Liz from New Zealand and Scott from the UK plan a presentation about Stone Point, a historical site in New Zealand.

questions.text: According to Liz, Stone Point played a key role in local history because

options.text: it was used for defence or attack purposes.
it was the landing point for the first Maori settlers.
it was developed as a commercial port.

questions.explanation: "It has been used by both Maori and European settlers as a place to shelter from attack or launch an attack for centuries." — defence or attack (A).

questions.text: Scott and Liz agree that Maori originally chose to inhabit Stone Point because of
questions.explanation: "Initially the fishing opportunities would have been the attraction." — supply of fish (B).

questions.text: Scott and Liz agree that using Maori terminology in their presentation

options.text: will be of interest to international students.
is required as a component of their research.

questions.explanation: "We need to keep most Maori terminology out of the presentation. Otherwise, a lot of the international students would not be able to follow us." — best avoided (C).

questions.text: When Scott mentions the engines at Stone Point, Liz advises him to

options.text: focus on the human aspect instead.
check the accuracy of specific dates.

questions.explanation: "I would not go into the technical side... it is more interesting to look at the impact Stone Point had on the people's lives at the time." — focus on the human aspect (A).

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the Berber peoples of North Africa and the nomadic Tuaregs of the Sahara.

groups.answerRule: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
groups.template:
The Berbers and Tuaregs of North Africa
Background
- Inhabited North Africa as long ago as the 7th century
- Bedouin Arab invasion in the 12th century destroyed their peasant economy
- Many left settlements to wander with animals through [[31]] and mountains
Three Types of Berber
- [[32]] nomads — farmers (lowlands in winter, mountains in summer)
- Fully nomadic Berbers — moved between oases
- Oasis-settled Berbers — grew fruit and vegetables; made [[33]] for cooking
- Increasingly relied on [[34]] for transport in the dry Sahel
Settled Berber Life
- Built single-story stone houses by quarrying local rock
- Small-scale industries (pottery, weaving) done by women
- Men met in the village [[35]] to discuss affairs
Tuaregs
- Tents made from up to 40 goatskins sewn together
- When skins not available, mats made of [[36]] or palm leaves were used
- Society was strictly hierarchical — from nobles down to laborers whose ancestors were [[37]]
- Men wore a [[38]] veil in front of women, strangers and in-laws (called ‘blue men’)
Modern Tuaregs
- Numbers in the Sahel have declined due to droughts
- Many moved into Burkina Faso to find new grazing lands for their [[39]]
- Mali government employs Tuaregs as [[40]] for desert tourism

questions.explanation: "Many Berbers left their settlements to lead a nomadic life by wandering with their animals through the deserts and across the different mountains."
"Some became farmers cultivating the lowlands in the winter and grazing their flocks of animals in the mountains during the summer. They are called seasonal nomads."
"A third group settled by the oases and grew fruit and vegetables... as well as making olive oil, which they used for cooking."
"The Berbers relied more and more on camels for transporting their families and their goods."
"The life of a settled community was governed by the men, who met regularly in the village square to discuss affairs and make decisions."
"If the skins were not available, they wove mats made of grass or palm leaves and hung them over a frame."
"Ranging from nobles or aristocrats downwards to laborers whose ancestors had once been slaves."
"All adult males wore a dark blue veil in the presence of women, strangers and in-laws."
"Those whose animals were fortunate enough to survive have moved away from the Southern Sahara into Burkina Faso in order to find new grazing lands for their herds."
"The tourism department of the Mali government employs some Tuaregs who act as guides."

parts.transcript:
A lecture on the Berber peoples of North Africa and the nomadic Tuaregs of the Sahara.
▶ 18:07[Narrator] Now turn to section four on page seven. Section four. You will hear part of a lecture on rural development.
▶ 18:18[Narrator] First you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
▶ 19:04[Narrator] Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
▶ 19:11Lecturer: Good morning everyone. Now you'll remember that last week we looked at the migration of people from the interior of West Africa to various coastal towns with special reference to Ghana.
▶ 19:23Lecturer: Today we're going to focus on the people known as the Berbers who live in North Africa.
▶ 19:29Lecturer: The Berbers inhabited this part of Africa as long ago as the 7th century, and their society was based on tribes which were scattered throughout a number of countries: Algeria, Morocco, Libya, and Mali.
▶ 19:43Lecturer: However, at some point in the 12th century, the area was invaded by Bedouin Arabs. These people destroyed the Berbers' peasant economy.
▶ 19:52Lecturer: As a result, many Berbers left their settlements to lead a nomadic life by wandering with their animals through the deserts and across the different mountains.
▶ 20:02Lecturer: Over the centuries, many Berbers migrated to other countries like Spain and France to work as laborers, taking with them their culture and traditions, and their descendants remain there until this day.
▶ 20:15Lecturer: Not all the Berbers led a fully nomadic life. There were three different groups. Some became farmers cultivating the lowlands in the winter and grazing their flocks of animals in the mountains during the summer.
▶ 20:29Lecturer: They are called seasonal nomads. Some Berbers who led a completely nomadic life tended to move from one oasis to another. A third group settled by the Oases.
▶ 20:41Lecturer: And grew fruit and vegetables like dates and eggplants, as well as making olive oil, which they used for cooking. Traditionally, Berbers kept cattle, sheep, and goats, together with oxen, mules, and horses.
▶ 20:56Lecturer: Now, in the Sahel region of North Africa, that's the area south of the Sahara Desert, the region became and still is becoming increasingly dry and arid.
▶ 21:06Lecturer: So the Berbers relied more and more on camels for transporting their families and their goods. How did these different groups of people survive in such harsh conditions? Where did they live?
▶ 21:20Lecturer: Well, Berbers who stayed put in one place built single-story stone houses for protection by quarrying the local rock.
▶ 21:29Lecturer: Whereas nomadic Berbers carried their homes with them and erected temporary tents, settled Berbers developed various small-scale industries such as pottery making and weaving, but these tasks were generally left to the Berber women.
▶ 21:44Lecturer: As you might expect, though, the life of a settled community was governed by the men, who met regularly in the village square to discuss affairs and make decisions.
▶ 21:58Lecturer: Now let's turn to the Tuaregs, who belong to a nomadic Berber group and move mainly in the central and western Sahara Desert, north of the river Niger.
▶ 22:09Lecturer: The word Tuareg comes from the Arabic Tawarek and means God forsaken. Desert Tuareg carried tents made of strips of goatskins sewn together.
▶ 22:21Lecturer: As many as forty skins were needed to make a complete tent. If the skins weren't available, they wove mats made of grass or palm leaves and hung them over a frame so that the tent looked like a humped dome.
▶ 22:35Lecturer: Tuareg society was traditionally very feudal and organized as a strict hierarchy, ranging from nobles or aristocrats downwards to laborers whose ancestors had once been slaves.
▶ 22:50Lecturer: Tuaregs were famous for their warlike qualities and fierce independence. In fact, one of the greatest insults was to suggest to a Tuareg that his father had died in his bed and not while fighting.
▶ 23:04Lecturer: Tuareg men were sometimes called blue men, as all adult males wore a dark blue veil in the presence of women, strangers and in laws.
▶ 23:13Lecturer: Legend had it that a Tuareg man couldn't be recognized unless he was wearing this veil. But this custom of the veil began to disappear as more and more Tuaregs became urbanized and moved to the towns.
▶ 23:27Lecturer: I mentioned earlier how dry the Sahel region has become, and there have been very severe droughts over the past 30 years. This has meant that the number of Tuaregs living in the area has declined.
▶ 23:39Lecturer: Those whose animals were fortunate enough to survive have moved away from the Southern Sahara into Burkina Faso in order to find new grazing lands for their herds.
▶ 23:50Lecturer: If there's one city which people associate with the Sahara Desert, it's probably Timbuktu. But what most people don't know is that Timbuktu was founded by Tuareg nomads almost a thousand years ago.
